content.title: About
content.content: Snowpeas are young pea pods that can be eaten fresh, cooked, or after a small amount of fat has been added. They have a mild sweet flavor, a crisp texture when raw, and become tender after cooking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Snowpeas belong to the legume family and represent an early stage of pea development.
Fresh pods are rich in B‑vitamins and vitamin C.
Cooking retains most nutrients as long as the pods are not over‑cooked.
Adding a little oil improves absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.
Snowpeas are popular in Asian cuisine, used in salads, soups, and stir‑fries.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports healthy digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: Provides about 5 g of protein per 100 g, useful for vegetarians.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Contains vitamin C, folate, iron, and magnesium, which aid immunity and metabolism.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Helps maintain stable blood sugar levels when consumed in moderation.

items.title: Antioxidant compounds
items.content: Rich in flavonoids that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to peas.

items.title: Gas formation
items.content: Legumes can cause increased gas in sensitive people.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid may reduce mineral absorption if consumed in excess.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fresh snowpeas can be eaten raw in salads, added to smoothies, or as a snack. Cooked pods work well in soups, stews, and side dishes. Lightly sautéing with a bit of oil makes them aromatic while preserving nutrients.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh pods in the refrigerator in a perforated bag; they stay crisp for 3‑5 days. Cooked or sautéed snowpeas should be kept in an airtight container in the fridge and used within 2‑3 days.

tongue-pot-roast-puerto-rican-style.title: Tongue Pot Roast, Puerto Rican Style

content.title: About
content.content: Tender beef tongue slow‑roasted in a fragrant sauce made with tomatoes, olive oil, vinegar, garlic, oregano and spices typical of Puerto Rican cuisine. The dish is slightly tangy, sweet and spicy, perfect as a main course or a hearty appetizer.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beef tongue is a traditional ingredient in Caribbean and Latin American cooking.
In Puerto Rico the tongue is often marinated in an “adobo” of vinegar, garlic, oregano and spices before cooking.
Tongue is rich in collagen, which is touted for skin and joint health.
The dish is commonly served with rice, beans and fried plantains.
Traditionally the tongue is boiled for several hours before roasting to develop a crisp crust.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Tongue provides a complete source of animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamin complex
items.content: It contains B12, B6, niacin and riboflavin, which support nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Rich in iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals are important for blood formation and immune health.

items.title: Collagen source
items.content: Collagen from tongue may help maintain healthy skin, hair and joints.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: When served without sugary sides, the dish fits well into low‑carb eating plans.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to beef or veal, including the tongue.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: The sauce often contains soy sauce or added salt, so people with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Cooking challenges
items.content: Improper cooking can leave the tongue tough or undercooked, increasing the risk of food‑borne illness.

items.title: Cholesterol
items.content: Tongue contains cholesterol; those with heart concerns should consume it in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice the roasted tongue thinly and serve hot with rice, beans, fried plantains or a fresh salad. A squeeze of lime and chopped cilantro adds brightness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C before serving.
